fr:title.text: Verification of the CVM Algorithm with a Functional Probabilistic Invariant

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Verification of the CVM Algorithm with a Functional Probabilistic Invariant

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: For this week, there is progress in several directions.

Firstly, re-familiarised definitions of a \mathbb {K}-fibration, in particular the case where \mathbb {K} is a subcategory of Poset. Fibration ensures the existence and uniqueness of Cartesian liftings of morphisms in the underlying category, which is inherited by \mathbb {K}. These liftings are seen concretely as a predicate transform, which connects between predicate objects in the total category. More generally, in effectful settings, we deal with Monad liftings, of the form (\dot T, \dot \eta , \dot \mu ). The monad lifting transforms predicates into certain effectful versions. From this background, one can perform weakest precondition calculation in an effectul setting, which provides a semantic basis for Floyd-Hoare style logics. There is a general formula to build Cartesian monad liftings in the case of domain fibrations, and an associated wp operator. This is presented rather vaguely in as \tau \circ \Phi \circ f, but in more detail in the followup journal version.

Secondly, the work of John Li on a probabilistic separation logic is investigated. Understand that discrete conditioning is viewed as modal operator, and independence can be viewed as separation. In this sense, random variable is seen as resource ownership, with possibly the same underlying probability space. His recent ambition is to develop wp for free in the sense of .

Thirdly, the work of Justin Hsu on probabilistic relational Hoare logic is investigated. The workings of pRHL in constructing couplings syntactically, is understood. In addition, several examples are worked out, including equivalence of output distributions, stochastic dominance, and (more briefly) convergence. There is suspiciously no mention of a weakest precondition calculus. I wonder if such calculus can be constructed and given a categorical wp interpretation in the sense of Aguirre.

Fourthly, I started to introduce a Hoare logic for reasoning with higher-order functional invariants in probabilistic programs. The inspiration comes from a recent proof of tail bound for the CVM algorithm . Logical formulas of the form C \models \forall h\in SomeFuncSet. E[h(X)] \leq g(h), where g is some simple transformation on h. This would automatically generalize the usual Chernoff bounds; in fact judgments of this form is a realization of Cramer-Chernoff method. This would easily generalize a few useful identities in the first-order Hoare logic and its pre-expectation calculus. After this logic is introduced (including its assertion language and proof rules), a next step is to proof soundness and completeness with respect to some semantics. In particular, completeness is harder. Possible semantic models include the Schanuel topos and the BI-hyperdoctrine. They would be interesting to implement because of the probabilistic content.
